# Digest B — Phil 1:1–26 (Hansen Philippians PNTC)

## Coverage

- **Cache file:** `slice_B_1_1-26.txt` (exclusive)
- **Briefed range:** I. Greetings and Grace (1:1–2); II. Prayers for Partners (1:3–11); III. Reports of Gospel Ministry (1:12–26: progress of gospel; motives for preaching; courage to honor Christ by life or death)
- **Actually read:** Full cache slice, lines 1–395 (section headers through Hansen’s closing paragraph on 1:26 / mission report)
- **Structure covered:**
  - I. GREETINGS AND GRACE (1:1–2) — lines 1–44
  - II. PRAYERS FOR PARTNERS (1:3–11) — lines 46–162
  - III. REPORTS OF GOSPEL MINISTRY (1:12–26)
    - A. Progress of the Gospel (1:12–14) — lines 165–201
    - B. Motives for Preaching Christ (1:15–18a) — lines 203–236
    - C. Courage to Honor Christ by Life or by Death (1:18b–26) — lines 238–393
- **Overflow past briefed verses:** None. Slice ends at Hansen’s synthesis of 1:12–26; does not enter 1:27ff.
- **Note:** Hansen refers ahead to 1:27–30, 2:1–11, 3:x, 4:x for illustration; those verses are not the primary exegesis of this slice, but claims about *this* passage that cite them as support are recorded when Hansen makes them here.

## Claims

### Christocentric threefold name in the prescript
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** The threefold repetition “Christ Jesus… Christ Jesus… Lord Jesus Christ” presents the letter’s central, uniting theme around the person of Christ; the blessing anticipates the Christ hymn’s finale (2:11).
- **Quote:** "The threefold repetition of the name - Christ Jesus, Christ Jesus, the Lord Jesus Christ - presents the central theme that reappears throughout the letter and unites everything around the person of Christ."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:1–2; Hansen on 1:1–2 (slice ll. 8–9)
- **Wiki targets:** [[philippians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[christ-hymn]], [[kyrios]], [[exaltation-christology]]
- **Type:** structure | theme

### Paul follows Greek letter form; first person singular throughout
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** Beginning with his own name follows common Greek letter form; though the letter is first-person singular, Timothy is included in the salutation.
- **Quote:** "By beginning the letter with his own name, Paul follows the common form of Greek letters in his day. Although Paul writes the entire letter in the first person singular, he also includes Timothy in the salutation."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:1; Hansen on 1:1 (slice l. 11)
- **Wiki targets:** [[philippians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[timothy]]
- **Type:** fact | structure

### Why Timothy is named: secretary and confirmation
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** Timothy is probably included as Paul’s secretary taking dictation and to assure the Philippians that the letter’s points are confirmed by Timothy, known from Paul’s first visit (Acts 16:1–12).
- **Quote:** "Timothy is probably included because he served as Paul's secretary by writing down Paul's dictation of this letter. Timothy may also be mentioned because Paul wanted to assure the Philippians that the points made in this letter were confirmed by Timothy, whom they knew from the time of Paul's first visit to Philippi (Acts 16:1-12)."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:1; Hansen on 1:1 (slice l. 11)
- **Wiki targets:** [[timothy]], [[paul-apostle]], [[philippi]], [[philippians]]
- **Type:** position

### Timothy as rare example of Christ-like humility
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** Paul speaks of Timothy with warmth (2:22); Timothy’s sacrificial service echoes the Christ hymn (2:6–8) and models Christ-like humility and service.
- **Quote:** "Paul's description of Timothy's sacrificial service to others clearly echoes Paul's hymn to the self-giving love of Christ (2:6-8). From Paul's perspective, Timothy was a rare example of Christ-like humility and service."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:1 (with 2:22; 2:6–8); Hansen on 1:1 (slice l. 11)
- **Wiki targets:** [[timothy]], [[christ-hymn]], [[humility-and-pride]], [[paul-apostle]]
- **Type:** theme | position

### “Servants” instead of “apostle”: unusual shared title
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** Paul usually introduces himself as apostle; here he makes no apostolic self-reference and uses the same title for both Paul and Timothy—literal “slaves.”
- **Quote:** "This is a significant departure from Paul's customary self-designation. Paul usually introduced himself as an apostle of Christ Jesus. But in this letter he makes no reference to his apostolic position. … he uses the same title for both himself and Timothy. Their work together was that of 'slaves,' the literal meaning of the term servants."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:1; Hansen on 1:1 (slice ll. 13–14)
- **Wiki targets:** [[paul-apostle]], [[timothy]], [[philippians]], [[humility-and-pride]]
- **Type:** structure | position

### Slave title: total subjection; Philippi as Roman colony context
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** In a Roman colony like Philippi, slaves’ lack of freedom made the status ignominious; Paul’s later reference to Christ’s slave-obedience (2:7–8) shows the title means total subjection to the master’s will.
- **Quote:** "In a Roman colony like Philippi, some slaves did menial work while others had great responsibilities in civil service. But in either case their lack of freedom and their subservience to their masters who owned them made their position as slaves ignominious compared to those who were free. Paul's reference later in this letter to Christ's own obedience as a slave, obedience even to death on a cross (2:7-8), indicates that Paul's use of the title of slaves for himself and Timothy points to their total subjection to the will of their master."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:1 (with 2:7–8); Hansen on 1:1 (slice ll. 15–16)
- **Wiki targets:** [[philippi]], [[paul-apostle]], [[christ-hymn]], [[humility-and-pride]]
- **Type:** theme | position

### Servant title as high privilege and OT honorific
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** Being servants of Christ Jesus is high privilege (sharing Christ’s slave-form; serving the exalted Lord); in the Greek OT “servant” titles Moses, Joshua, and David as servants of the Lord—humble yet honored.
- **Quote:** "Paul considered the position that he and Timothy had as servants of Christ Jesus to be a high privilege. … In the Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures, the term 'servant' is used as a title for Moses, Joshua, and David, who were each called servants of the Lord."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:1; Hansen on 1:1 (slice ll. 17–19)
- **Wiki targets:** [[paul-apostle]], [[timothy]], [[christ-hymn]], [[kyrios]]
- **Type:** theme | position

### Shared servant title models unity against envy/rivalry
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** The servant title points to Paul’s view of relationships: freely accepted service unites; envy, rivalry, and selfish ambition ruin relationships; Paul exemplifies the attitude of the slave-form (2:5–8).
- **Quote:** "Relationships are ruined by envy, rivalry, and selfish ambition (1:15-17; 2:3), but they will thrive when friends humbly serve each other before looking out for their own interests (2:3-4). At the beginning of his letter, Paul exemplifies the attitude he calls for all believers to have, the attitude of the one who accepted the form of a slave (2:5-8)."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:1 (with 1:15–17; 2:3–8); Hansen on 1:1 (slice l. 21)
- **Wiki targets:** [[humility-and-pride]], [[philippians]], [[christ-hymn]], [[partnership]]
- **Type:** theme

### “Christ Jesus” as messianic double name without defense
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** The double name expresses belief that Jesus is the Messiah; Paul presupposes rather than defends messiahship and builds theology on it; the hymn portrays humility unto death and sovereignty as divine Lord.
- **Quote:** "The double name, Christ Jesus, expresses Paul's belief that Jesus is the Messiah. In fact, the messianic role and work of Jesus was such a presupposition for Paul that he does not defend it but builds his theology upon it."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:1 (with 2:6–11); Hansen on 1:1 (slice l. 23)
- **Wiki targets:** [[paul-apostle]], [[christ-hymn]], [[exaltation-christology]], [[kyrios]]
- **Type:** theme | position

### “God’s holy people” = all believers; holiness by union, not performance
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** “God’s holy people” is Paul’s common designation for all believers—not a super-spiritual elite; holiness is separation/consecration based on Israel’s call, inherent in calling and position *in Christ*, not earned by social position or moral performance.
- **Quote:** "Such people are not in a special club of super-spiritual Christians. … Their holiness is inherent in their calling and position in Christ. It is not earned by social position or moral performance, but by union with Jesus Christ."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:1; Hansen on 1:1 (slice l. 25)
- **Wiki targets:** [[philippians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[justification]]
- **Type:** theme | position

### Address to “all” aims to heal divisions
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** Addressing *all* and repeating “all” promotes unity and includes opposing factions; Euodia and Syntyche (4:2) and others fighting could not miss being embraced as one.
- **Quote:** "By addressing his letter to all, Paul shows that he is promoting the unity of all rather than recognizing any social or moral distinctions. The repetition of his references to all in the opening part of his letter emphasizes Paul's concern to heal the divisions in the church by including opposing factions within his embrace."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:1 (with 4:2); Hansen on 1:1 (slice l. 25)
- **Wiki targets:** [[philippians]], [[humility-and-pride]], [[partnership]]
- **Type:** theme | position

### “In Christ Jesus” parallel to “at Philippi”: residence metaphor
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** Parallel prepositional phrases clarify *in Christ*: the community lives *in Christ* as it resides *at Philippi*; the phrase needs fresh evaluation in each context and can mean personal experience of Christ, corporate objective position, or ethical activity by indwelling power.
- **Quote:** "All God's holy people are in Christ Jesus and at Philippi. The parallelism of these two prepositional phrases clarifies the meaning of this first instance of Paul's use of the important in Christ phrase in this letter. … At this point the phrase in Christ tells us where the Christian community lives, just as the phrase in Philippi tells us where the church resides."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:1; Hansen on 1:1 (slice ll. 27–28)
- **Wiki targets:** [[philippians]], [[philippi]], [[paul-apostle]], [[dyadic-devotion]]
- **Type:** theme | position

### Philippi as Roman colony: Via Egnatia, foundation, citizenship background
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** Philippi sat in NE Macedonia on the Via Egnatia; founded 42 B.C. as colony for Roman veterans after Brutus/Cassius’ defeat; reestablished after Actium (31 B.C.) as Colonia Iulia Augusta Philippensium; Augustus repopulated with Roman soldiers and Italian farmers.
- **Quote:** "The residents of Philippi lived in the northeastern corner of Macedonia on the famous Via Egnatia, a major Roman road. The city was founded in 42 B.C. as a colony for Roman veterans after the defeat of Brutus and Cassius by Mark Antony and Octavian (later Caesar Augustus). Later the city was reestablished as a Roman colony, Colonia Iulia Augusta Philippensium, after Augustus defeated Mark Antony in the battle of Actium in 31 B.C."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:1; Hansen on residence in Philippi (slice ll. 29–30)
- **Wiki targets:** [[philippi]], [[philippians]], [[citizenship]]
- **Type:** fact

### Philippi culture as analogy: koinonia and citizenship
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** Paul uses Philippi’s social realities as analogies: common *koinonia* in friendships/business resources theology of partnership in Christ; Roman citizenship undergirds exhortation to live as citizens worthy of the gospel (1:27) and “citizenship in heaven” (3:20).
- **Quote:** "The common experience of partnership (koinonia) in friendships and business in Philippi was a resource for Paul's theology of partnership in Christ (1:5, 7; 2:1; 3:10; 4:14, 15). Another prominent aspect of life at Philippi was the privilege of Roman citizenship. The concept of citizenship is the basis for Paul's exhortation to live as citizens in a manner worthy of the gospel of Jesus Christ (1:27) and his reminder that our citizenship is in heaven (3:20)."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:1 (anticipating 1:5, 1:27, 3:20); Hansen (slice l. 33)
- **Wiki targets:** [[philippi]], [[partnership]], [[citizenship]], [[philippians]]
- **Type:** theme | structure

### Overseers and deacons: only (non-Pastoral) joint mention; two purposes
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** Only time (except Pastorals) Paul mentions overseers and deacons together; no further title-reference in the letter. Purposes: (1) leaders administered financial support and sent Epaphroditus (4:18)—letter as “thank you”; (2) commission leaders to ensure the church follows instructions and resolve conflicts (esp. Euodia/Syntyche 4:2) so gospel is embodied in humility and unity.
- **Quote:** "this is the only time in Paul's letters, except for the Pastorals, where overseers and deacons are mentioned together as leaders of the church. … Paul directed his opening greetings to leaders (overseers and deacons) in the church because they were the potential solution to the problem of disunity in the church."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:1 (with 1:5, 1:27, 4:2, 4:15–18); Hansen on 1:1 (slice ll. 35–36)
- **Wiki targets:** [[philippians]], [[epaphroditus]], [[monepiscopate]], [[partnership]], [[humility-and-pride]]
- **Type:** position | structure

### Plural leadership; leaders “with” not “over” the church
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** Two inferences: (1) plurality of shared leadership, unity of the group; (2) leaders addressed as *together with* the church, not over it—part of the church; humility call (2:3–4) especially for them; humility emphasis starts with Paul/Timothy as servants.
- **Quote:** "First, he refers to a plurality of leaders. The responsibilities of leadership were shared by a group of leaders in the church. … Second, the leaders are not addressed as those who are over the church but rather as those who are together with the church. … these leaders are part of the church and serve together with the church."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:1 (with 2:3–4); Hansen on 1:1 (slice l. 37)
- **Wiki targets:** [[philippians]], [[monepiscopate]], [[humility-and-pride]], [[paul-apostle]]
- **Type:** position | theme

### Grace and peace: not empty formula; theological essence
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** Grace adapts Greek “greetings”; peace echoes Jewish Shalom; combination reflects Greek/Jewish cultural intersection; used in all Paul’s letters but not empty cliché—condenses essence of his theology: unmerited saving work of God in Christ brings peace (harmonious relations with God and each other); bookends with 4:23 and 4:7, 9.
- **Quote:** "Often referred to as a common formula or social convention in Paul's letters, this phrase of greeting is anything but an empty cliche for Paul. In fact, it expresses in condensed form the essence of his theology. His message is one of grace and peace: grace, the unmerited, undeserved saving work of God in Christ Jesus brings believers into peace, harmonious relationships with God and with each other."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:2 (with 4:7, 9, 23); Hansen on 1:2 (slice ll. 39–40)
- **Wiki targets:** [[philippians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[justification]]
- **Type:** theme | position

### Source of grace/peace: redefined monotheism / Shema including Jesus
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** Source is God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ; after meeting the risen Christ, Paul’s faith included Jesus within the Shema—redefined monotheism expressed in the Christ hymn concluding “Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (2:11).
- **Quote:** "Before meeting the risen Christ, Paul's central affirmation of faith was the Jewish creed known as the Shema: 'Hear, O Israel, the LORD our God, the LORD is one.' After his encounter with Christ, Paul's faith included Jesus Christ within the Shema: 'The Lord (Jesus Christ) (and) God (our Father), the Lord is one.' This redefined monotheism is expressed in the great Christ hymn (2:6-11)."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:2 (with 2:6–11); Hansen on 1:2 (slice l. 41)
- **Wiki targets:** [[kyrios]], [[dyadic-devotion]], [[exaltation-christology]], [[christ-hymn]], [[paul-apostle]]
- **Type:** theme | position

### Opening themes: partnership of servants, inclusive all, gospel and community
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** Inclusion of Timothy as partner-servants, address to all in Christ, and reworded Shema introduce gospel of Christ and community in Christ; “highly exalted” Christ is center; only way to maintain unity is focus on Christ Jesus; threefold name flows from “to live is Christ.”
- **Quote:** "In his opening greetings, Paul begins to express the main points of his letter. His inclusion of Timothy in a partnership of servants of Christ Jesus, his inclusive address to all in Christ Jesus, and his rewording of the Shema to include the Lord Jesus Christ with God the Father as the common source of grace and peace introduce the themes of the gospel of Christ and the community in Christ."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:1–2; Hansen summary (slice ll. 43–44)
- **Wiki targets:** [[philippians]], [[partnership]], [[dyadic-devotion]], [[christ-hymn]]
- **Type:** structure | theme

### Thanksgiving-prayers: real prayers, not mere formula/rhetoric
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** Though Paul has a predictable thanksgiving form after greetings (except Galatians) that functions rhetorically as introduction, the Philippians would not have heard these as formulaic devices; they are authenticated by intimate connection to Paul’s experience and specific gifts/needs of recipients.
- **Quote:** "But surely the Philippians would not have heard these prayers as formulaic epistolary expressions and classical rhetorical strategies calculated to secure their goodwill. These prayers are authenticated as real prayers, not merely formulas or rhetorical devices, by the way they are so intimately related to Paul's experience with the Philippians and his concerns for them expressed throughout the letter."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:3–11; Hansen intro to II (slice l. 53)
- **Wiki targets:** [[philippians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[partnership]]
- **Type:** position | structure

### Letter as “thank you” tied to Epaphroditus’s gifts (4:18)
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** “I thank my God” relates to the formal-receipt language at the letter’s close for gifts via Epaphroditus (4:18); from beginning to end the letter needs to be read as a “thank you,” yet more deeply from personal experience of God’s grace (“my God”).
- **Quote:** "This thanksgiving is directly related to the close of the letter where Paul writes what reads like a formal receipt: I have received full payment and have more than enough; I am amply supplied, now that I have received from Epaphroditus the gifts you sent (4:18). From beginning to end, the letter needs to be read as a 'thank you.'"
- **Locus:** Phil 1:3 (with 4:18–19); Hansen on 1:3 (slice l. 55)
- **Wiki targets:** [[philippians]], [[epaphroditus]], [[partnership]], [[paul-apostle]]
- **Type:** structure | theme

### Translation debate: “I remember you” vs “your remembrance of me”
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** Some insist “I thank my God for all your remembrance of me” (gifts as remembrance), fitting 4:x and grammatically possible; Hansen judges traditional “every time I remember you” wins: in six other NT uses of the noun with genitive, the genitive is object of remembering; reversing runs counter to Paul’s pattern and leaves object unexpressed.
- **Quote:** "Although this translation receives strong support, the weight of evidence for the traditional reading - every time I remember you - decides the case in its favor. … Any translation that reverses this so that the Philippians remember Paul runs counter to the consistent pattern of Paul's own use of this noun with a genitive."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:3; Hansen on 1:3 (slice ll. 57–61)
- **Wiki targets:** [[philippians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[partnership]], [[g-walter-hansen]]
- **Type:** position

### Four elements of Paul’s prayer practice (1:4)
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** (1) Frequency—*always* thanks God for them in every prayer; consistent gratitude possible only with Godward focus on God’s work. (2) For *all*—no exclusion despite 4:2 fighting; prayer sees unity. (3) Specific urgent requests (*deēsis*) combined with thanksgiving (cf. 1:19; 4:6). (4) With *joy*—first of fourteen joy notes; joy = confidence in God who began and will finish the good work of *koinonia*.
- **Quote:** "This is the first of fourteen times that the joy note sounds in this letter. … So the source of joy is the God who began the work of partnership (koinonia) in the gospel (1:5) and who will complete that work. The nature of joy is confidence in God, who begins and finishes his good work."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:4–6; Hansen on 1:4 (slice ll. 63–69)
- **Wiki targets:** [[joy]], [[partnership]], [[philippians]], [[paul-apostle]]
- **Type:** theme | structure

### Spirituality chain: memory → petition → thanksgiving → joy
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** Memory of friends → urgent requests → thanksgiving → joyful praise forms a chain reaction in Paul’s spirituality.
- **Quote:** "Here we see a chain reaction in Paul's spirituality: memory of friends leads immediately to urgent requests for their needs; these petitions prompt him to give thanks to God for his friends; thanksgiving to God lifts him to express joyful praise to God."

- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** Greek *koinonia* connotes close relationships involving mutual interests and sharing (marriage/family, friendships, business, property, citizenship, religious organizations); six references in Philippians; major purpose of the letter is to transform *koinonia* experience in light of life in Christ.
- **Quote:** "Standing behind the English word partnership, the Greek word (koinonia) connotes a variety of close relationships 'involving mutual interests and sharing.' … A major purpose of this letter is to transform the experience of koinonia in the light of life in Christ."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:5; Hansen on 1:5 (slice ll. 73–74)

### Partnership = friendship in gospel + participation in salvation benefits
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** First, *koinonia* is close friendship sharing common faith; Aristotle: all friendship involves *koinonia*; passion language (1:7–8); friendship from first day of gospel; mutual participation in grace/peace through cross and resurrection; confirmed by *koinonia* of Spirit (2:1) and sufferings of Christ (3:10); “brothers and sisters” nine times.
- **Quote:** "The kind of koinonia enjoyed by Paul and the Philippians in their partnership in the gospel is first of all a close association as friends who share a common faith in the gospel. According to Aristotle, 'All friendship involves koinonia.'"

### False dichotomy: salvation participation vs evangelism cooperation
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** Interpreting “partnership in the gospel” *only* as participation in salvation *or only* as evangelism cooperation is a false dichotomy; personal appropriation enables support for propagation; faithfulness in proclamation evidences participation by faith.
- **Quote:** "A false dichotomy is set up by some who interpret the phrase partnership in the gospel to mean participation in salvation and by others who take this phrase as a reference to cooperation in the work of evangelism. For if there had not been personal appropriation of the gospel in the first place, there would not have been support for the propagation of the gospel."

### Breadth of partnership activities (not only belief or money)
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** Philippians as fellow-partners in defending/confirming the gospel (1:7); participation via prayers (1:19), suffering (1:27–30), radiant witness (2:15–16), Epaphroditus’s mission (2:25–30), regular financial support (4:10–18); must not reduce to belief alone or finance alone; “first day” = reception of gospel.
- **Quote:** "It is important to appreciate the breadth of the Philippians' involvement in this partnership in the gospel so that it is not reduced to either their belief in the message of salvation in Christ or their financial support of Paul's mission to preach the gospel."

### 1:6 “good work” is corporate koinonia, not only individual salvation
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** Widely applied individualistically (God will complete my salvation), but that misses connection to *koinonia*: the good work God began is formation of a corporate partnership in the gospel; threatened by external opposition (1:28) and internal conflict (4:2); survival depends on God as founder who will complete every true *koinonia* until the day of Christ Jesus.
- **Quote:** "Philippians 1:6 is widely interpreted as a basis for personal confidence: God began the good work of salvation in me, and he will complete that good work in me. Of course, the good work of God includes God's work of salvation in the individual. But as true as that individualistic application of the text is, it misses the connection of God's good work to koinonia. The good work that God began was the formation of a corporate entity: the partnership (koinonia) in the gospel."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:5–6 (with 1:28; 4:2); Hansen on 1:6 (slice ll. 81–83)
- **Wiki targets:** [[partnership]], [[philippians]], [[g-walter-hansen]], [[justification]]
- **Type:** position | theme

- **Claim:** Paul keeps eyes on day when every knee bows (2:9–11) and Savior transforms citizens of heaven (3:20–21); bright light of that day filled Roman prison darkness; new community will be perfect/complete; vision inspires present life; hope strengthens endurance.

### Phronein (1:7): feel/think/attitude; ten uses; model for unity
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** TNIV “feel” fits intense affection but *phronein* also means thinking, concern, opinion, attitude; ten occurrences map positive attitudes (unity, Christ-mind, mature view, concern) vs negative (earthly mind of cross-enemies); Paul’s positive *phronein* for all exemplifies right attitude vs envy/rivalry/selfish ambition; models friendship love for Euodia/Syntyche and like-mindedness appeals.

### “I have you in my heart” vs NRSV “you hold me in your heart”
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** Greek allows either (both pronouns accusative with infinitive). NRSV favored by focus on faithful partners and gifts; TNIV supported by whole prayer report of Paul’s love, climaxing in oath of 1:8—passage is about Paul’s heart for believers; Hansen prefers TNIV: Paul has them in his heart (heart = center of inner life; commitment to live/die for friends, cf. 2 Cor 7:3; 2:17).
- **Quote:** "This passage is all about Paul's heart for the believers. So the TNIV translation correctly views Paul as the subject: I have you in my heart. Though geographically distant, Paul held them in his heart. Paul was not a friend who followed the common practice: 'out of sight, out of mind.'"
- **Locus:** Phil 1:7–8; Hansen on 1:7 (slice ll. 95–97)
- **Wiki targets:** [[philippians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[partnership]], [[g-walter-hansen]]

### Chains; defending and confirming as legal trial terms
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** First mention of chains; repeated 1:13, 14, 17—Paul cannot shake free of them. “Defending and confirming” are legal terms for court speech of defense and validation of the gospel; technical legal sense confirmed by 1:16 (chains for defense of gospel); vindication through suffering becomes major theme.
- **Quote:** "The prospect of his trial is reflected in his use of two legal terms: defending and confirming. Paul viewed his trial as an opportunity to make a 'speech of defense' that would lead to the 'validation' of the gospel. … his use of the same terms in his recognition that he was in chains for the defense of the gospel (1:16) shows that these terms have a technical legal sense in this context."

### Boasting in Christ Jesus on account of Paul (1:26)
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** *kauchēma* = pride/exulting/boasting (not mere “joy”); two *en* phrases: Christ as object/sphere and Paul as occasion/means of boasting; ultimately Christ is reason, Paul’s mission specific occasion; total identification (to live is Christ) means boasting in Paul leads to boasting in Christ.
- **Quote:** "Both lines of interpretation agree that Christ is the ultimate reason for boasting and Paul's mission is the specific occasion for boasting. Paul's total identification of his life with Christ (For to me, to live is Christ!) means that boasting in Paul really leads to boasting in Christ, the source of Paul's life."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:26 (with 2:16; 3:3); Hansen on 1:26 (slice ll. 387–389)
- **Wiki targets:** [[philippians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[joy]]
- **Type:** theme | position

### Return visit and imprisonment origin: Rome / Caesarea / Ephesus options
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** Expected return visit challenges chronology: Rome origin requires changed plans (Rom 15:23 east finished; 2 Cor 1 shows Paul could change plans); Caesarea origin → Philippi en route to Rome; Ephesus origin → visit documented in 2 Cor 1 / Acts 20. Origin must be decided on other bases than travel plans alone.
- **Quote:** "No matter what position one takes regarding the origin of Paul's letter to the Philippians, reasonable explanations can be given for Paul's plans to make a return visit to Philippi. The question of origin has to be decided on other bases than Paul's travel plans and itineraries."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:26; Hansen on 1:26 (slice l. 391)
- **Wiki targets:** [[philippians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[philippi]]
- **Type:** position | fact

### Section synthesis 1:12–26: no shame in chains; pride in mission; glory to Christ
- **Speaker:** Hansen
- **Claim:** Mission report: chains advanced gospel (palace guard; bold proclamation; Christ exalted by life or death); therefore no need for shame—pride in what Paul accomplishes in chains; all glory to Christ.
- **Quote:** "Therefore, there is no need to be ashamed of Paul's imprisonment. Instead everyone should take pride in all that is being accomplished by Paul, even while he is in chains. And everyone should give Christ all the glory for all that he has done in and through Paul."
- **Locus:** Phil 1:12–26 close; Hansen (slice l. 393)
- **Wiki targets:** [[philippians]], [[paul-apostle]], [[joy]], [[partnership]]
- **Type:** structure | theme

## Key structural points

1. **I. 1:1–2** — Christocentric salutation: shared “slave” title (not apostle); all holy people *in Christ* / *at Philippi*; plural overseers & deacons *with* the church; grace & peace as theological condensed gospel; Shema-including redefined monotheism.
2. **II. 1:3–11** — Thanksgiving-intercession as real partnership prayer: *koinonia* from first day; God completes corporate good work to day of Christ; *phronein* + heart + co-partnership in grace (giving/suffering); love abounding in knowledge/insight → discern best → pure/blameless community → fruit of (ethical) righteousness through Christ → doxology.
3. **III.A 1:12–14** — Disclosure formula; *prokopē* of gospel via chains; palace guard; emboldened majority.
4. **III.B 1:15–18a** — Same brothers, same Christ-message; envy/rivalry/selfish ambition vs goodwill/love; joy that Christ is preached; reject anti-Paul-faction reconstruction of Philippi.
5. **III.C 1:18b–26** — Future joy; *sōtēria* as present Spirit-empowered bold exaltation of Christ in the body; live = Christ / die = gain; torn between depart-with-Christ and necessary remaining; progress & joy in the faith; boasting in Christ through reunion.

## Open questions / absences

- **Exact imprisonment city:** Not settled in this slice; Hansen uses “Roman prison” / palace-guard framing heavily and reviews Rome–Caesarea–Ephesus options at 1:26 without deciding from itinerary alone.
- **Identity of envious preachers:** Hansen explicitly says only certain they are inside the church and not content-false teachers; motive-details speculative.
- **Full text-critical apparatus** for “word” vs “word of God” (1:14): noted briefly; no exhaustive MS list beyond early/Majority/diversity comments.
- **Full six *koinonia* catalogue** for the whole letter: counted and thematically introduced; detailed treatment of each occurrence beyond 1:5, 7 is largely deferred.
- **Euodia/Syntyche narrative detail:** used as division foil, not full exegesis (belongs later).
- **Not present in this range:** full treatment of 1:27 citizenship paraenesis; Christ hymn body (2:6–11) as primary text; new-perspective debates as such (though 1:11 / 3:9 righteousness balance is set up); monepiscopate history beyond plurality/with-not-over inference; Lydia, Silas narratives (not in this slice’s exegesis).
- **Overflow:** None past 1:26.
